claim: The best static analysis tools plateau at around 50-60% detection rates for security vulnerabilities, per NIST SATE evaluations.
stance_target: structural/static analysis alone is insufficient for zero-hallucination quality control; needs requirement-aware review
quoted_support: The NIST SATE evaluations found the best static analysis tools plateaued at around 50-60% detection rates for security vulnerabilities.

claim: Roughly half of security defects are implementation bugs (pattern-matchable, caught by static analysis) and the other half are design flaws (intent violations invisible to code-only analysis).
stance_target: code review quality gates must incorporate requirements/intent, not just pattern matching
quoted_support: Roughly 50% of security defects are implementation bugs, and the other 50% are design flaws... design flaws are about intent: The system's architecture doesn't enforce the security properties it's supposed to enforce.

claim: A 2024 empirical study testing five static analysis tools against 815 real vulnerability-contributing commits found that 22% of vulnerable commits went entirely undetected and 76% of warnings in vulnerable functions were irrelevant to the actual vulnerability.
stance_target: static/SAST tooling has a measurable detection ceiling and high false-positive noise
quoted_support: A 2024 study by Charoenwet et al. (ISSTA 2024) confirmed this is still the case: They tested five static analysis tools against 815 real vulnerability-contributing commits and found that 22% of vulnerable commits went entirely undetected, and 76% of warnings in vulnerable functions were irrelevant to the actual vulnerability.

claim: Missing Authorization (CWE-862) is a design-flaw class of vulnerability that structural code review cannot detect without a written requirement, and ranked #9 on the 2024 CWE Top 25 most dangerous software weaknesses.
stance_target: intent-based/negative-requirement review catches security gaps structural review misses
quoted_support: That's CWE-862: Missing Authorization, and it rose to #9 on the 2024 CWE Top 25 most dangerous software weaknesses. That's not a coding error! It's a missing requirement.

claim: Deriving null-handling requirements from community-reported GitHub issues enabled an AI tool to find and get merged a real bug in Google's Gson library where duplicate keys were silently accepted when the first value was null.
stance_target: requirement-derivation from historical issues/chat logs surfaces bugs invisible to structural review
quoted_support: The playbook derived null-handling requirements from Gson's own community—GitHub issues #676, #913, #948, and #1558, some dating back to 2016—then used those requirements to find that duplicate keys were silently accepted when the first value was null... The fix was merged as https://github.com/google/gson/pull/3006, confirmed by Google's own test suite.

claim: Spec-driven development (SDD) describes implementation detail (the 'how') but not purpose (the 'why'), which limits an AI's ability to verify whether code fulfills its intended purpose across unlisted edge cases.
stance_target: spec-driven development vs requirements engineering for AI code verification
quoted_support: An SDD spec describes the how—what the implementation should look like... But it's not enough for verifying them... When the AI knows the purpose, it can evaluate whether the code actually fulfills that purpose across all the edge cases, not just the ones the spec explicitly listed.
